say.text: A 58-year-old man has a groin lump that is tense, tender and irreducible. He is vomiting and looks unwell.
What is your first move?

choices.label: Try gentle, then firm, manual reduction
Resuscitate him, then take him to emergency surgery
Order an ultrasound of the groin first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the lump is doing to its contents. A tense, toxic swelling changes the plan before any test or reduction.
Tempting, but it fails here: a tense, toxic swelling may hold dead bowel, and pushing can drive that bowel back in.
Reducing is the reflex for every groin lump you have seen, which is why it feels right. Check viability first.

sure_note.text: You were sure of reducing. That reflex suits a reducible hernia; with strangulation signs it is the wrong first step.

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: an ultrasound answers whether an occult hernia is present. This one is clinically evident.
The scan delays the operation the bowel needs. Time goes to resuscitation and surgery, not to imaging.

sure_note.text: You were sure of imaging. Tests help an unclear groin; a tense, toxic lump needs the surgeon, not a scan.

say.text: The right first step is resuscitation, then emergency surgery.
Strangulation is a bowel-viability emergency. Resection of any non-viable bowel is decided once the surgeon sees it.
The sac is tense and the bowel may be dead. Why is forceful reduction avoided here?

choices.label: It turns the hernia into an irreducible one, delaying surgery
It can push gangrenous bowel back, or cause reduction en masse
It is acceptable after analgesia, once the sac has relaxed
It only causes pain and a haematoma in the groin

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: the hernia is already irreducible, and the danger is the bowel, not the sac.
A forceful push can reduce sac and contents together while the constriction is still there.
Tempting, but it fails here: analgesia changes how the patient feels, not whether the bowel is alive.
The step that comes first is checking viability at surgery, not a gentler push.
Tempting, but it fails here: pain and bruising are minor. The serious harm is pushing dead bowel back in.
Gangrenous bowel reduced into the abdomen is what makes this an emergency.
The push is dangerous because of what it does to the bowel: it can drive gangrenous bowel back, or reduce sac and contents together with the constriction persisting.
That is why strangulation goes to theatre, not to the reduction chair.
A 6-month-old boy has a reducible right groin swelling that appears on crying.
What is the operation of choice?

choices.label: Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair of the posterior wall
High ligation and excision of the sac alone
Herniorrhaphy that repairs the posterior wall with tissue
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the defect is in a six-month-old. Is the back wall of the canal the problem, or something else?
Tempting, but it fails here: mesh is the adult answer, and the adult model makes you add a wall repair.
A child's defect is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall. Nothing needs mesh.

sure_note.text: You were sure of an adult repair. Check the age first; the operation follows the child's defect.

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: a posterior wall repair is the textbook extra step, and a child does not need it.
In a child the operation is herniotomy alone, with high ligation and excision of the sac.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a wall repair. In a child the wall is not the defect, so it is not repaired.

say.text: The operation is high ligation and excision of the sac alone.
That fits the defect: a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so nothing else is repaired.
Why does a child's hernia need no posterior wall repair?

choices.label: Children's tissues are too fragile to hold sutures or mesh
The sac is a patent processus and the posterior wall is normal
A mesh would restrict growth of the abdominal wall
The posterior wall is repaired later, at puberty

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: fragility sounds right if you picture a small adult with a weak wall.
A child's wall is normal; the defect is the open sac, so there is no wall to repair.
Tempting, but it fails here: growth is a real surgical worry, yet no mesh is placed in a child's groin.
The posterior wall is not the defect, so there is nothing for a mesh to fix.
Tempting, but it fails here: a staged repair assumes the wall will need work later.
Nothing is staged. A child's operation is herniotomy alone, and the posterior wall is not the defect.
The defect is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so only the sac is dealt with.
Herniotomy alone is therefore the whole operation for a child.
Mesh reinforcement of the posterior wall is called what?
Tempting, but it fails here: herniorrhaphy is also a posterior wall repair, so it sounds like the same job.
Herniorrhaphy uses the patient's own tissue. Mesh reinforcement is hernioplasty.
Tempting, but it fails here: herniotomy is the simplest word, and it feels like the general one.
Herniotomy is sac excision alone; it adds no repair and no mesh.
Hernioplasty is reinforcement of the posterior wall with a prosthetic mesh.
The ladder: herniotomy excises the sac, herniorrhaphy adds the patient's own tissue, hernioplasty adds mesh.
A 35-year-old man has a primary, unilateral, reducible inguinal hernia. The surgeon has no laparoscopic training.
Which repair is best?

choices.label: Totally extraperitoneal (TEP) repair, for less pain and faster return
Bassini repair, the classic open operation
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: laparoscopy is the newer route, with less pain and faster return to work.
It needs general anaesthesia and a learning curve. The qualifiers here point to open mesh.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the newer route. Read the qualifiers before choosing it: bilateral and recurrent favour it, this case does not.

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: Bassini sounds like the textbook classic, so it is an easy recall.
Older question papers keyed Bassini, but current practice is mesh repair. Bassini is a tension repair that has been replaced.
Read the qualifiers first: primary or recurrent, one side or both, and whether the surgeon is trained for laparoscopy.
The operation is Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair.
Open mesh suits a primary unilateral hernia when the surgeon is not trained for laparoscopy. Laparoscopy is preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernia.
In which scenario is laparoscopic repair clearly preferred?

choices.label: Primary unilateral hernia in a fit adult
Bilateral hernia in a fit adult
Elderly man unfit for general anaesthesia

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: laparoscopy feels like the modern default, so a single hernia can look like its case.
A primary unilateral hernia does not make laparoscopy the preferred route; that rests on bilateral or recurrent disease.
Tempting, but it fails here: laparoscopy looks gentler, so an elderly patient can seem a good fit.
Laparoscopy needs general anaesthesia, which is the problem for an unfit patient.
Bilateral hernia is the scenario where laparoscopy is preferred.
Recurrence after an open repair is the other one. A primary unilateral hernia is not.
Which pairing is right: the nerve most at risk in open repair, then the nerve most at risk in laparoscopic repair?

choices.label: Open: lateral femoral cutaneous; laparoscopic: ilioinguinal
Open: ilioinguinal; laparoscopic: lateral femoral cutaneous
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: the thigh nerve feels like the open risk because it is the famous groin nerve. It is the laparoscopic one.
Open repair injures the ilioinguinal nerve, causing numbness at the root of the penis and scrotum.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the swap. Tie the nerve to the approach: open dissection risks the ilioinguinal, laparoscopy the thigh nerve.

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: the ilioinguinal is the nerve you learn first, so one nerve feels enough for both approaches.
The setting word decides it: the laparoscopic route puts the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure one nerve covers both. Each approach has its own nerve, so read the setting word first.

say.text: Ask where each approach dissects, then which nerve lies in that field.
Open repair risks the ilioinguinal nerve; laparoscopic repair risks the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
Open: numbness at the root of the penis and scrotum. Laparoscopic: meralgia paraesthetica.
Which structures lie in the triangle of doom?

choices.label: Femoral nerve and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: both triangles are no-tack zones, and the groin is full of nerves, so nerves feel right.
The triangle of doom is vascular. Its nerves belong to the triangle of pain, lateral to the gonadal vessels.
Tempting, but it fails here: the femoral branch is a famous nerve of the groin, so it feels like a doom structure.
That nerve lies in the triangle of pain. The triangle of doom holds the external iliac vessels.
The external iliac vessels lie in the triangle of doom, bounded by the vas deferens medially and the gonadal vessels laterally.
A tack here risks the vessels, which is why this triangle is called doom.
After a transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) repair, a man has chronic groin pain and thigh numbness. The tack sat lateral to the gonadal vessels, below the iliopubic tract.
Which triangle was the tack in?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, but it fails here: both triangles are no-tack zones, so one name feels as good as the other.
Doom sits medial to the gonadal vessels and holds vessels. Check which side of the gonadal vessels the tack fell.

sure_note.text: You were sure of doom. Doom is the vascular triangle; the tack here fell on the other side of the gonadal vessels.

say.text: Look at which side of the gonadal vessels the tack fell, and which structures it caught.
The triangle of pain lies lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract. It holds the nerves.
Nerve damage here is what the case describes: pain and numbness from a tack in this triangle.
